title: Nonlocal Magnonic Cat States in Hybrid Magnon-Qubit Architectures
authors: Urmimala Dewan, Roson Nongthombam, Sampreet Kalita, Amarendra K. Sarma
abstract: The quantum superpositions of coherent states offer an alternative to the conventional qubit-based encodings by harnessing the large Hilbert space available in bosonic modes, including those realised in microwave and optical cavities, magnons, and mechanical resonators. Beyond their advantages for local information processing, establishing long-distance quantum networks for such bosonic states is crucial for scalable quantum communication and distributed quantum computation. In this work, we propose an entanglement-swapping-based protocol to generate a bipartite magnonic cat state shared between spatially separated subsystems. Each subsystem comprises a hybrid architecture consisting of a superconducting transmon qubit coupled to a yttrium iron garnet (YIG) sphere that supports magnon modes. By performing a projective Bell-state measurement on the qubits, the initially established magnon-qubit entanglement is coherently transferred to the remote magnon modes, resulting in a nonlocal magnonic cat state. For experimental characterisation of the gener- ated states, we perform quantum state tomography through reconstruction of the Wigner function using joint displaced parity measurements of the magnon modes. Our scheme provides a feasible route towards realising long-distance magnonic entanglement and contributes to the advancement of hybrid quantum network architectures.
summary: The paper proposes an entanglement-swapping protocol to generate nonlocal magnonic cat states across separated subsystems. It utilizes hybrid architectures combining transmon qubits and YIG magnon modes, demonstrating how projective measurements can transfer entanglement over distance. This work advances the feasibility of long-distance quantum networking using solid-state bosonic systems.
main_problem: The goal is to generate a bipartite magnonic cat state shared between two spatially separated subsystems.
main_result: The authors propose an entanglement-swapping protocol that successfully transfers magnon-qubit entanglement to create a nonlocal magnonic cat state, demonstrating a feasible route for long-distance quantum networking.
method: The protocol involves generating initial magnon-qubit entanglement, using a microwave cavity interaction to generate qubit Bell states, and finally performing a projective Bell-state measurement on the qubits to project the remote magnon modes into the desired bipartite cat state.
model_or_system: The system is a hybrid architecture combining superconducting transmon qubits with Yttrium Iron Garnet (YIG) spheres supporting magnon modes. The dynamics are modeled using a Hamiltonian and evolved via the Lindblad master equation to account for dissipation.
key_observables: Fidelity ($F_{ eta}$ or $F_{cat}$), Entanglement Negativity ($	ext{EN}(ho)$), and the joint Wigner function of the bipartite cat state.
important_parameters: The effective detuning ($\Delta$), coupling strength ($g$), and decoherence rates ($\gamma_m, \gamma_q$) are key parameters governing the dynamics.
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on the Rotating-Wave Approximation (RWA), and comparisons between analytical results and simulations must account for dissipation and measurement noise.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of the hybrid system, show fidelity/entanglement evolution over time, and display the analytically calculated Wigner functions for the four possible bipartite cat states.
paper_structure: The paper details the Hamiltonian formulation, describes the entanglement-swapping protocol using Bell state measurements, provides analytical derivations for the resulting Wigner functions, and validates the scheme through simulation results.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses quantum networking by utilizing solid-state magnonic systems (YIG) coupled to superconducting qubits. The use of cat states in a long-distance setting is highly relevant for scalable quantum communication protocols.
